title: Cluster Architecture
summary: Control plane and node components, how they talk, and the ports they use.

blocks.text: A cluster is a **control plane** plus a set of worker machines called **nodes**. Nodes run the Pods that make up your application. Every cluster needs at least one worker node to run Pods.
The control plane makes global decisions, such as scheduling, and reacts to cluster events. For example, it starts a new Pod when a Deployment's `replicas` field is not satisfied.
In production, the control plane usually runs across multiple computers and the cluster runs multiple nodes, for fault tolerance and high availability.

rows: Exposes the Kubernetes API; the front end of the control plane
Consistent, highly-available key-value store for all cluster data
Watches for new Pods with no node and picks a node for them
Links the cluster to a cloud provider's API (optional)

items: **kube-apiserver** scales horizontally: you can run several instances and balance traffic between them.
**etcd** holds all cluster data, so have a backup plan for it.
**kube-scheduler** considers resource requirements, hardware/software/policy constraints, affinity and anti-affinity, data locality, inter-workload interference and deadlines.
**kube-controller-manager** runs many controllers in one process, compiled into a single binary. Examples: Node, Job, EndpointSlice and ServiceAccount controllers.
**cloud-controller-manager** is absent when you run on your own premises or in a learning environment on your PC.

rows: Agent on each node; makes sure the containers in its PodSpecs are running and healthy
Maintains network rules on nodes that implement Services
Runs containers and manages their lifecycle

items: The kubelet does **not** manage containers that Kubernetes did not create.
kube-proxy uses the OS packet-filtering layer when one is available; otherwise it forwards traffic itself.
Some network plugins implement Service forwarding themselves. With one of those, nodes do not need kube-proxy.
Supported runtimes include containerd, CRI-O, and any other implementation of the **CRI** (Container Runtime Interface).

blocks.text: Addons use Kubernetes resources (DaemonSets, Deployments, and so on) to provide cluster-level features. Their namespaced resources belong in the `kube-system` namespace.

items: **DNS**: not strictly required, but all clusters should have cluster DNS. Containers automatically include it in their DNS searches.
**Web UI (Dashboard)**: a general-purpose web UI for managing and troubleshooting the cluster.
**Container resource monitoring**: records time-series metrics about containers.
**Cluster-level logging**: saves container logs to a central store.
**Network plugins**: implement the **CNI** spec, allocate Pod IPs and let Pods talk to each other.

sections.heading: How nodes and the control plane talk
sections.sourceTitle: Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane

blocks.text: Kubernetes uses a **hub-and-spoke** API pattern. All API usage from nodes and their Pods terminates at the API server; the other control plane components do not expose remote services.

items: Node → control plane traffic is secure by default. The API server listens on a secure HTTPS port, typically 443, with client authentication enabled.
Pods reach the API server through a service account. Kubernetes injects the root certificate and a bearer token.
API server → kubelet connections are used for fetching Pod logs, attaching to running Pods, and port-forwarding.
By default the API server does **not** verify the kubelet's serving certificate. Use `--kubelet-certificate-authority` to make it verify.
SSH tunnels are deprecated; the **Konnectivity service** is their replacement.

blocks.text: A node joins the API server in one of two ways: the kubelet **self-registers** (the preferred pattern, enabled by `--register-node`, which defaults to true), or someone adds a Node object manually.

items: `kubectl cordon` marks a node unschedulable. New Pods are not placed there; existing Pods are not affected.
Node heartbeats come in two forms: updates to the Node's `.status`, and **Lease** objects in the `kube-node-lease` namespace.
If a node becomes unreachable, the node controller sets its `Ready` condition to `Unknown`.
Node status contains addresses, conditions, capacity/allocatable, and info.

blocks.text: DaemonSet Pods tolerate unschedulable nodes, so they keep running on a cordoned node.
These are defaults and all of them can be overridden. A common example: the API server is sometimes moved to 443, or put behind a load balancer that listens on 443.

sections.heading: Ways to run the control plane

rows: Components run directly on dedicated machines/VMs, often as systemd services
Components run as static Pods managed by the kubelet. kubeadm uses this approach
The control plane runs as Pods inside the cluster itself
A cloud provider runs the control plane for you

blocks.text: Tools such as kubeadm, kops and Kubespray each lay out and manage the components in their own way.

questions.stem: A new Pod stays unassigned to any node. Which control plane component is responsible for assigning it?

options.explanation: The scheduler watches for Pods with no assigned node and selects one for them.
The kubelet runs Pods once they're bound to its node; it doesn't choose nodes.
etcd stores cluster data; it makes no scheduling decisions.
kube-proxy maintains network rules for Services.

questions.stem: Which component is Kubernetes' backing store for all cluster data?

options.explanation: etcd is the consistent, highly-available key-value store for cluster data.
The API server exposes the API, but it persists data in etcd.
It runs controllers; it doesn't store cluster state.
The runtime runs containers on a node.

questions.stem: Which components run on every node? Select 2.

options.explanation: The kubelet is the agent on each node.
Every node needs a runtime to run containers.
The scheduler is a control plane component.
etcd is part of the control plane.

options.text: Horizontally: run more instances and balance traffic between them
options.explanation: The docs describe kube-apiserver as designed to scale horizontally.

options.text: Only vertically, with more CPU on one machine
options.explanation: It is explicitly designed to scale by adding instances.
You can run several instances.
Not described; instances share the same backing store.

questions.stem: Your cluster runs on-premises with no cloud provider. Which component will it not have?

options.explanation: On-premises and learning clusters do not have a cloud controller manager.
Every cluster runs core controllers via kube-controller-manager.
Scheduling is needed in every cluster.
Every node runs a kubelet.

questions.stem: True or false: The kubelet manages containers on its node that were started outside of Kubernetes.

options.explanation: The docs say the kubelet doesn't manage containers which were not created by Kubernetes.
Correct. It only manages containers described in the PodSpecs it receives.

options.explanation: Network plugins implement the CNI spec.
